title: Blue River Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Blue River wells have a 133-foot median depth, with typical completed-well costs of $14,600-$25,300.
h1: Blue River, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Buying land or a home in Blue River means understanding the local well record before you rely on a driller’s estimate. Permitted wells within five miles show a mountain-bedrock setting, with most wells completed in unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers. The available records include 3,674 permitted wells, although only 2,069 are recorded as constructed and 1,223 report a pump yield.

Nearby records from Breckenridge, Copper Mountain, Frisco, Keystone, Alma, and Dillon can provide useful comparison points, but a neighboring well is not a guarantee for your parcel. Local fractures, elevation, access, and the exact site can change both the drilling depth and the water supply.

sections.heading: Blue River Well Depth: What the Mountain Ground Requires
sections.html:
The median permitted well depth near Blue River is 133 feet. The middle half runs from 80 to 200 feet, so a bid based on the median is only a starting point: half of the reported wells fall outside that range. The 90th-percentile depth is 282 feet, and the deepest record reaches 700 feet.

Depths cluster in the moderate range. Thirty-three percent of wells are under 100 feet, while 59% fall between 100 and 300 feet. Another 8% are between 300 and 600 feet, with no recorded wells at 600 feet or more. Most permits identify unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, so granite and gneiss fractures—not a uniform sand layer—control where drilling finds water.

sections.heading: How Much Water a Blue River Well Can Produce
sections.html:
Reported pump yield has a median of 10.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 7.0 and 12.0 gallons per minute. That is a useful range for planning a home, but it is not a promise for a new hole. Seventy percent of reported wells produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, and 20% report more than 15 gallons per minute.

Ten percent fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, while no recorded wells are listed under 1 gallon per minute. Ask for the permitted use, the pumping test method, and any storage-tank design. A household well may legally be limited by its permit, and the general exempt-well pumping limit is 35 gallons per minute; that limit does not mean the aquifer will deliver that amount.

sections.heading: Blue River Water Levels and the Long Record
sections.html:
Among the 306 wells reporting static water level, the median depth to water is 80 feet below the surface. The middle half is 50 to 120 feet. That matters when a contractor sizes the pump and estimates the lift from the standing water level to the pressure system.

The decade series does not show a sustained decline in this record. Median depth to water was 80 feet in the 1970s, 80 feet in the 1980s, 71 feet in the 1990s, 80 feet in the 2000s, 80 feet in the 2010s, and 80 feet in the 2020s. These are measured-well medians, not a site-specific guarantee. Seasonal conditions, pumping nearby, and the fracture connected to your well can still produce a different result.

sections.heading: Who Has Drilled Near Blue River, and When
sections.html:
Permit activity is spread across decades, with the largest period in the records occurring during the 1990s, when 968 permits were issued. The record shows 726 permits from the 2000s, 371 from the 2010s, and 293 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2026, so this is not only an older well district.

The most active drillers in the records are Golden Eagle Drilling Corporation, Shelton, Joe Wayne, with 728 records; Buena Vista Drilling, Shelton, William L, with 541; and Arrow Drilling Co., Berglund, Paul R., with 287. These counts describe permit records, not current availability, workmanship, or a recommendation. Confirm licensing, insurance, references, and the proposed construction details before hiring.

sections.heading: What a New Blue River Well May Cost
sections.html:
Blue River’s fractured mountain bedrock is the main cost driver. The local drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the 133-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $8,600 to $13,300.

A finished system—including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical—is modeled at about $14,600 to $25,300 at that median depth. Treat those figures as planning numbers, not a fixed proposal. A deeper hole, difficult access, extra casing or grout, longer trench runs, difficult electrical work, or a failed hole can change the final bill. Have the bid state what happens if the driller must continue beyond the assumed depth or cannot establish an adequate supply.

sections.heading: Blue River Risks: Water Quality, Yield, and Building Limits
sections.html:
The local map includes 9 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 9 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites, and 1,521 historic mine features within about 10 miles. Those mapped sites do not prove contamination at a particular parcel, but they justify a site-specific water test and a review of nearby mine and cleanup records. Test for the contaminants relevant to the property’s history and location.

Fractured rock can produce a strong well next door and a weak or dry hole on the same slope. Before building, confirm the permit’s household use, well location, septic separation, and available space for the drainfield. An exempt household-use well is not a substitute for checking water rights; an over-appropriated basin may require an augmentation plan for some uses.

sections.heading: Buying or Building on a Blue River Lot
sections.html:
Start with the DWR permit, construction report, pump-yield record, and static-water measurement for the actual property. The nearby statistics are encouraging on yield, but only 1,223 wells report a pump yield and only 306 report a static water level, so the database is incomplete. Ask the seller for recent production, treatment, repair, and water-quality records.

Have a driller review access for a rig, likely casing and grout, the proposed well location, and the cost of a deeper search. Compare several nearby wells, especially around Breckenridge, Frisco, and Dillon, without assuming they match your lot. For a new home, coordinate the well, septic system, driveway, electrical service, storage, and building envelope before closing. A well that works on paper still needs a practical site plan.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Blue River, Colorado?
faq.a: The median permitted well depth within five miles of Blue River is 133 feet. The middle half runs from 80 to 200 feet, while the 90th percentile is 282 feet. Thirty-three percent are under 100 feet and 59% are between 100 and 300 feet. The deepest record is 700 feet.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Blue River?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $65 to $100 per foot in fractured mountain bedrock. At the 133-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $8,600 to $13,300. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $14,600 to $25,300.

faq.q: How much water do Blue River wells produce?
faq.a: Reported wells have a median pump yield of 10.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 7.0 and 12.0 gallons per minute. Seventy percent produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. Ten percent report 1 to 5 gallons per minute, so a pump test and storage plan still matter.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Blue River?
faq.a: The records do not establish that every well is safe to drink. Within about 10 miles, the map includes 9 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 9 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites, and 1,521 historic mine features. Test the property’s water, review local site history, and use treatment based on laboratory results.

faq.q: Are Blue River wells getting deeper or losing water?
faq.a: The reported static-water medians do not show a sustained decline: they were 80 feet below surface in the 1970s, 80 in the 1980s, 71 in the 1990s, and 80 in each later decade listed. Only 306 wells report a static level, however, so the series is regional and incomplete rather than a guarantee for a particular lot.
